newsitem.title: PERU: Peru crash inquiry to focus on "crazy" computer.
newsitem.headline: Peru crash inquiry to focus on "crazy" computer.

text.p: Experts on Thursday began to investigate the crash of a Boeing 757-200 airliner in the Peruvian Pacific on Wednesday that killed all 70 aboard -- a crash that the government pinned on malfunctioning computers.

"It is not the first time that one of these planes has had this kind of fault," Transport Minister Elsa Carrera de Escalante told a news conference. "We have to find out why the computers went crazy."

A group of around 12 investigators from Boeing, engine maker Pratt & Whitney, the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration and the National Transporation Safety Board met with representatives from Aeroperu, the local airline that owned the plane.

A source close to the team of U.S. investigators said it was "very premature" to speculate about the cause of the crash and possible technical failures aboard the plane, which was in service for just three months.
Carrera said the inquiry would center on the computer failures aboard the jet based on recordings of a dramatic, 29-minute dialogue between pilot Eric Schreiber and Lima air traffic control.
"We've lost the basic instruments, both for height and for speed ... I've cut back the engines but we are accelerating," Schreiber said, according to Carrera. "Where am I? Over land or sea?"
Throughout the communications, Schreiber spoke with "incredible" calm, however, as he tried to steer his plane through dense fog back to Lima after setting off for Santiago, the minister said.

She added the government had requested help from the United States to recover the aircraft's two "black box" flight recorders, which were believed trapped inside the plane's trunk 180 yards (180 meters) below the ocean surface.
Boeing officials in Lima declined to comment on the investigative team or the cause of the crash.
The Peruvian navy -- leading a search that began before dawn on Wednesday -- continued to comb the site for remains of the wreckage.

Using helicopters, navy frigates and various private boats, rescuers had picked up by early Thursday afternoon 13 bodies floating in the icy waters. They also fished out passengers' clothes, shoes and personal documents along with seats and fragments of the plane's wing and fuselage.
"The problem is that the central part of the fuselage is too deep," said navy captain Augusto Zegarra, adding that most of the bodies were still trapped in the wreckage.
Meanwhile, relatives of the victims, who came from 11 countries, were arriving on Thursday in Peru to identify the few bodies recovered and visit the site where the rest were submerged.
Condolences poured in from around the world, including Pope John Paul II, French President Jacques Chirac, and the government of neighboring Chile, which lost 30 people in the crash.

Complaining bitterly at Peruvian authorities' failure to attend to them, one group of about 20 Chilean relatives traveled 34 miles (55 km) north of Lima to the coastal strip of Pasamayo. They hoped to travel the 45 miles (70 km) out to the crash zone, but found there was no sea transport for them.

Wednesday's crash, one of the worst in Peru's aviation history, came seven months after a Boeing 737 belonging to local Faucett airline crashed and killed all 123 people on board near Peru's second city, Arequipa.
Since 1967, a total of 601 people have been killed in air crashes in Peru. Aeroperu, privatized in 1993 and owned by Aeromexico, said it was operating flights normally on Thursday.

The crash was the third involving a 757, which had a perfect safety record from the time it entered commercial service in 1983 until last year, when an American Airlines 757 slammed into a mountain in Colombia, killing 159 people.
In February, a 757-200 crashed into the Caribbean shortly after taking off from the Dominican Republic, killing all 189 people aboard. Both crashes were blamed on pilot error.
